text:
The FPS/W bar diagrams are misleading and are too inaccurate:
1. Example: If a card makes it to only 25 avg FPS but little power consumption, then it would still "win" the comparison over a card that draws double the power but manages to deliver 45 avg FPS. Yet the better FPS/W ratio for the slow card makes it seem that it would be better when you wouldn't want to use it in the first place. A better way to present such information would be to provide the avg FPS data used along with the wattage as this typically weighs more to us users than a slightly better FPS/W ratio. The avg FPS used could easily be added inside the brackets like this (after I reversed the calculation since the FPS mentioned in that benchmark is off): Intel Arc B580 Ref [43.65FPS/145.5W].
2. Additionally showing only 1 decimal in the chart is too inaccurate. It should be two since (going with your graph) bars are of different length yet the number value displayed is the same.

text: If you upgrade to a newer GPU, just beware that they can only deliver their rated horsepower if slotted into a PCIe Gen 4 slot. So if you're still rocking the 1070, you're likely on PCIe Gen 3, possibly even 2. It might make sense to build a whole new computer, if that's the case. If not, go ahead and grab a B580. It's a significant jump in power from a 1070 and much cheaper than the 3060ti or 4060ti, unless you can get either one used. In which case, go ahead and grab a used 3060ti (in good condition). If you're unsure how to check what generation of PCIe your motherboard has, look up the model on the manufacturer's website.

text:
They won't kill their entire GPU division, because they need to keep making integrated GPUs. They might stop making discrete GPUs after this generation though. They will likely make very few B580 and B570s, because it is very likely that they are losing money on each one. 

A graphics card with a GPU die that's only a little smaller than the one used in the 4070 ti, made on the same process node, but with 45% less performance, is clearly not something which Intel can make a profit on. 250 USD is a good price, but it seems very unlikely that Intel will deem it worthwhile to keep making them in large enough quantities to allow them to be widely available for 250 USD for any significant length of time. 

Losing money in order to gain a bit of market share wouldn't be that valuable to them anyway, because it's not like people actually become that much more likely to buy the same brand again, and Intel would still need to offer good value in subsequent generations for people to still be willing to buy their graphics cards, which they are not likely to be able to do without losing money again the next time. People who are convinced to buy a graphics card because it had a great value are not typically the most loyal customers.

text:
Steve, I think it's a bit misleading to start your reviews talking about uplift from cards like the GTX 1060 and GTX 1070 when those cards largely exist in older machines supporting PCIe 3.0. The B580 only has 8 physical PCIe lanes, so the uplift you see on your test bench on those older cards won't be nearly as relevant until you account for the gimped bandwidth on PCIe 3.0 motherboards.

One of the biggest shortcomings of these cards is the 8 PCIe lanes, as these cards would have made great upgrades for machines 5 years old and older.

text:
This is a huge improvement
We're going from what is effectively 4 generations behind with the A770
To between 2 and 0.5 generation behind with the B580
That is a massive improvement for a single generation

Now that doesnt mean they've caught up, they're still using 4070/TI silicon to compete with the 4060TI(and sometimes the 4070), but they're doing it at a great price
author: @deegarkie5598

text:
To clarify
The A770 was effectively 2.5 nodes ahead of RTX 3000 (remember that Samsung 8nm is nowhere near TSMC 7nm/6nm and more close in performance to TSMC 12nm)
The A770 was in the same hardware class as the 3060TI/3070/4080
The A770 often struggled to beat the 3060

Contrast that to the B580
The B580 is on a slightly worse node than RTX 4000(same node but RTX 4000 is on an improved version)
The B580 is in the same hardware class as the 3060/4070/4070TI(B580 is slightly smaller but they're all in the 250-330mm 192 bit hardware class)
The B580 sometimes struggles with the 200mm-128 bit 4060TI, but it also sometimes sits between the 4070 and all other cards which means it is class competitive in those games though still notably slower(class competitive because there isnt a lower class card between them)

CES 2025 will be the unveiling of competition high end cards, --90/80 and -900/800 series cards which is a different market to this card. The budget focused cards don't tend to get announce or released until 6 months later (at least!) so this card is going to be sat there as a great value proposition for 6 months. I can see it ending up in A LOT of pre-builts; pre-builts can put in a cheaper similar performant card charge the same as they are now and make more margin.
Also given that competitors won't be announcing or releasing their budget lines for months, this release may delay it further if they are unable to be price/performance competitive. Which means this window was perfect for Battlemage, it's going to sat there slowly soaking up market share before nvidia release a more expensive "don't you want better" marketed card and AMD will struggle to win over people who will already have bought Battlemage.

text:
For the frame time graphs, I'd appreciate a marker line for ideal frame times of a couple relevant fps. It could totally be my "skill issue", might be clunky, or might be technically incorrect. However, I think it could help translate the information to minds stuck in fps while retaining the original information. I'd imagine most gamers are looking at an fps counter instead of a frame time counter.

Take 27:24 for example. Intellectually, I can know that "one-tenth of a second" is 10 fps. However, it had to go through several layers of translations and fact-checking. What is the frametime for 60? 30? 45? 120? I have no idea unless I look it up or try to divide. My instinct was "one-tenth" = 60 fps, probably confused from 60 seconds in a minute, one-tenth is 6 (very much my skill issue).

Basically, I can know that 100ms is bad. However, I can only imagine and visualize how bad it is while playing when thinking about a 60 fps spike to 10 fps.

I think it would be very interesting to check power when not in 3D, doing desktop usage, or maybe video playback (youtube for example)

The differences can be massive as with some cards, the memory has to wake up and doesn't have as finely grained power states as the GPU.

My 3080Ti often makes excursions to 100W, because VRAM needs 80W in it's fastest state, and it keeps switching up and down. All that while just decoding video and displaying at 4k.

text:
I'm impressed. First gen Arc was a bit of a letdown, though it was always unrealistic to have a strong start into a new market that Intel didn't have a lot of experience with. Even then, barring the initial launch which was rather poor, Intel had done a lot of work to improve on the driverside.
Now with second gen Arc seemingly starting strong and expecting Intel to work as hard on driver optimization as before, I'm actually a bit hopeful that by the time the next generation Intel GPUs hit the market, we may have a real tough competition in the entry and midrange GPU segment, which in turn hopefully either drives up performance, or costs down for the other product tiers as the competitors position their SKUs and pricing accordingly.

This is good news and I'm here for it. It is hilarious how Intel's CPU division is having such a thoroughly bad time (all of their own making to be sure), yet the GPU division in their infancy are actually set to add a lot of potential value to the market, both for the company and us consumers. Funny how that works out every once in a while.

text:
At the moment, the cards I have available for my builds are:
RTX3060Ti, RTX3080Ti, RX5700XT, and GT730.
It looks like this one is slightly worse than the RTX3060Ti across the board, and therefore I can assume it will also be worse than the 3080Ti.
The GT730 is a single slot, pcie 3x1, passively cooled, bus powered card that does display out and its graphics performance is good enough for operating system installers and terminal work. This is a double-slot 4x8 card with a fan that requires a separate power supply, so isn't a good replacement for that.
I don't know how it would compare with the RX5700XT. I mostly use that one for video encoding, where, on the specific workloads I use it for, it slightly outperforms the the RTX3080Ti. Intel seems to generally have a good track record on video encoding, but none of the reviews I've seen so far have looked at this particular card. Maybe I could use it there 🤷🏻‍♀.

text:
@Space97. ​ Helped who exactly? Like I can maybe think of a few examples. 

Copilot helps people code although when you deal with niche stuff it will rapidly fall off due to not enough data (curious if itd even work with something very niche like uiua). Your best bet then usually becomes what many people have done before (hopefully taking only their good coding practises with you)

It makes students write essays quicker I guess. But then they become reliant on it because they never learnt how to do it on their own. While not knowing how to write essays wont hurt much, personally I think being taught how to write them helped me a lot with messages like these so...


I guess on the student topic researching is probably AI's biggest thing going for it. Until you realise that due to its nature, it isn't going to always be correct which is something pretty important for researching things. (Hallucinations is what im talking about but ill get to that later)

And like all this is sure good but no it doesnt outweigh the downsides. 

First and foremost AI requires an absolutely insane amount of power. Going off of the international energy agency, a google request takes 0.3wh and a chatgpt request takes 2.9wh. Approximately 8.5 billion google searches are made per day which if you multiply both requests by that amount you get 2550mwh vs 24650mwh. Nearly a 10x increase for what nearly does the same thing, the thing you save on with chatgpt is not needing to click a few links?

And yeah you can say you dont need to click said few links. But then you get into another issue with the inherent (very very likely unsolvable) fact that this current generation of AI can and will hallucinate. So in all of its confidence it will give you the wrong answer and so people will take said answer and spread it around. 

All this also ignores the whole ethics side of things (oh god ethics in a youtube comment section). Do writers want large corporations to scrape what they write and then make money off of it? Since that is in a way whats happening. Sure you could argue that it learns like a human would etc etc etc but that completely ignores the scraping part of it and the fact that one might be fine with the average person doing it but not a large corporation doing the same.

So yeah. Like it does maybe have minor productivity improvements and I guess its cool? But at this current stage its not that good and frankly not even worth it. Whenever the next AI winter (go look at that on wikipedia) comes along maybe itll be better? Though the only way I can see AI actually being good is if you somehow directly teach it concepts via code but who knows if thats even possible lol.

text:
​ @peterlustig6888  My second message did not seem to be sent, at least I cannot see it so my bad if I send it twice but 

I do not think Christmas has anything to do with it,  at least not directly because the US also celebrate Christmas and the price is at MSRP, I think it is more of a supply thing.
Also I do not think the price will get better because of the tariff that are coming early next year, it might be worse.

Now why do I think it is a supply thing and it will last ? because Intel pay so much per chips compared to the competition. 
Intel use 5nm class silicon while AMD use 6nm (so 7nm family) 
Intel use 272 mm² of N5 silicon per die, AMD use 204 mm² of N6 
Die yield decrease exponentially has size increase 
From "The Information Network" the price per wafer is estimated at 12730 USD for a 5nm wafer and 9725 for a 7nm (so same familly has N6) the price are the one for 2024, 2025 is slightly lower 
We do not know the exact X and Y dimension of the die so it will be a guess but if we take Semi-Analysis die yield calculator and use value of 18x15mm (=270 mm²) for the Intel die and 15x14 (= 210 mm² so bigger than the 204 mm² and lower than the 272 mm² of intel but not by much) we can see intel would have a lot lower yield than AMD.
Something like  224 good die for AMD while intel would have 158 good die, the number themself mean nothing because I am not a TSMC insider and know the exact difference of N6 and N5 yield so it is more to give a idea of the range we are talking about. 
With just those number intel would pay around 80 USD per die while AMD would be around 45 USD close to half of it 
But the worse is that is not the end of the story, Jensen Huang go as "The More You Buy, The More You Save" I cannot imagine Intel ask for the same volume as AMD and we could speculate than Intel pay more per wafer than AMD. 

TLDR I think the supply will stay somewhat low because I do not think it make financial sense for Intel to sell this GPU, when taking into account all the logistic, the packaging, the VRAM, the AIB markup the reseller markup, all the other corporate expense you need to launch a product on top of the massive R&D and EUV mask cost, I just cannot see how this product itself make sense for Intel.

Now it would make even less sense to stop the dGPU effort so I am not saying they should cancel it, I am just saying they are probably not to catch the whole market with Battlemage because they are not ready for it 

I truly wish them the best but Battlemage right now need a more expensive node and bigger die, 50% more transistor and higher memory bus to beat a one year old AMD card... while selling it for lower than AMD

text:
​ @arcticowl1091  The only person looking stupid here is the one being incredibly confidently incorrect (you). Technically speaking EXE is a container format that is used to hold binary data, whether that data is meant to be used as windows software or anything else is irrelevant to the format itself. Similar applies for win32 as well. It's just standard libraries that you import into your code, not any OS specific functionality. If you look up the microsoft documentation for any random win32 functions you'll see towards the bottom of the page the name of the DLL that functionality is built into. One of the crucial things wine does is recreate these DLL's themselves and change the implementation to work with the Linux kernel syscalls. This means quite literally that it's possible to run an exe on Linux natively without having to emulate any functionality. In fact you could easily create an EXE that WON'T run on any version of Windows but will happily run under wine on Linux because you use a library not natively available on Windows.

Also the whole point of wine is attempting to run as much as it possibly can natively. That's why it was called "wine is not an emulator" to get away from people thinking it was emulator like you just did lol.
author: @jubjub727

text: Proton / wine only translate the windows api calls to the linux / vulkan native ones, there is no emulation being done. Its still using the native x86_64 instruction set. On top of that it creates the windows directory structure and provides nessesary dependencies, such as a native implementation of the win32 API. This is why older games tend to run better on linux than on the newest windows releases so yes games running through proton / wine are running natively.

It just doesn't have to emulate things unless there's specific functionality that can't be done with the Linux kernel. Although over time the Linux kernel has added functionality to speed up wine and reduce the amount of stuff that needs to be emulated.
